findings.issue_text: Write sync.Mutex held for the entire asset scan in dev mode, serializing all concurrent requests behind one global lock and stalling them on slow disk
Check-then-acquire pattern lacks a double-check under the write lock, so concurrent goroutines can both run the full asset scan with last-writer-wins instead of single-flight

New concurrency logic (double-checked locking) in GetWebAssets (webassets.go:38-52) has no test coverage, including fast path under concurrent readers, cache write under write lock, and partial initialization of EntryPointAssets

After acquiring the write lock in GetWebAssets (webassets.go:49-51), the cache is not re-checked, so concurrent cold-start requests each perform the full expensive asset computation instead of only one

Mutex guards the cached pointer, not the cached object; GetWebAssets returns the shared *dtos.EntryPointAssets directly, so any caller mutation races against concurrent readers — should return a deep copy on the cached fast path

Cache is globally keyed on nothing and the recompute condition only checks cfg.Env != setting.Dev, so different Cfg values or runtime license changes are never reflected until restart, with no invalidation story documented or tested

Double-checked-locking pattern is incomplete: the write-lock path never re-checks entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the lock, so N concurrent first requests serialize and redundantly recompute the asset scan, wasting work and extending tail latency

In Dev mode, the function takes and holds the exclusive write lock for the entire filesystem scan on every request even though the Dev read path bypasses the cache, serializing all Dev requests unnecessarily

Missing cache re-check after acquiring the write lock in webassets.go: concurrent cold-start requests serialize on entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock() but each still rebuilds assets, causing N sequential filesystem scans instead of one (partial stampede)
Global cache ignores the *setting.Cfg parameter of GetWebAssets: first caller's cfg determines cached result, so later callers with different Cfg silently receive wrong assets
Returned *dtos.EntryPointAssets is a shared pointer handed to every request: any handler mutation corrupts responses process-wide, with lock guarding the pointer but not the contents

GetWebAssets holds the exclusive write lock across the entire asset-scan/rebuild work in Dev mode, serializing concurrent Dev-mode requests on a potentially slow filesystem walk; the lock scope is wider than the race requires (compute-then-swap under lock would suffice)

GetWebAssets returns the same shared *dtos.EntryPointAssets pointer to all callers across goroutines, so any handler mutating the struct would cause a data race (pre-existing, not introduced by the diff)
Read-then-lock pattern is a benign double-checked read of a pointer that can result in redundant work, though not a security failure
Behavioral change to GetWebAssets (replacing racy unsynchronized global read with lock-based double-checked caching) has no accompanying test changes in the diff

New double-checked-lock pattern in webassets.go takes the global write Lock unconditionally on cache miss, including every call in Dev mode, risking serializing all Dev-mode requests behind a global mutex (lock convoy on every / asset fetch); it's unclear whether the write-locked body re-checks the cache, so double-computation may occur
No test exists anywhere in the diff covering concurrent Dev-mode calls for the new caching pattern
Double-checked locking in GetWebAssets does not re-read entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the write lock, so concurrent first-callers in non-Dev mode can each rebuild the cache unnecessarily
Missing double-check of entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock(), causing concurrent cold-start requests to serially perform redundant full asset scans
Cannot verify whether the freshly computed result is stored back into the cache inside the lock due to truncated diff — a store outside the critical section would be a race

goldens.comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.

In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Write sync.Mutex held for the entire asset scan in dev mode, serializing all concurrent requests behind one global lock and stalling them on slow disk

adjudication.rationale: In `GetWebAssets`, after the initial `RLock`/read of `entryPointAssetsCache`, the code takes `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` with a `defer entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Unlock()` before computing `result` (the rest of the function, including any asset scanning, happens while holding the write lock). Because the early-return is gated by `cfg.Env != setting.Dev`, in dev mode it will always proceed into the locked section, so concurrent requests will be serialized behind this global write lock for the duration of the work. This is a real performance/concurrency concern grounded in the diff, though not a direct correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Check-then-acquire pattern lacks a double-check under the write lock, so concurrent goroutines can both run the full asset scan with last-writer-wins instead of single-flight

New concurrency logic (double-checked locking) in GetWebAssets (webassets.go:38-52) has no test coverage, including fast path under concurrent readers, cache write under write lock, and partial initialization of EntryPointAssets

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows new locking around the global cache (RLock/RUnlock fast path, then Lock with defer Unlock), but it does not show any tests or test changes either way. From this diff alone you cannot verify whether there is or isn’t coverage for concurrent readers/writers, nor can you substantiate claims about "partial initialization" of EntryPointAssets. The finding asserts absence of tests, which is not checkable from the provided snippet.

adjudication_records.issue_text: After acquiring the write lock in GetWebAssets (webassets.go:49-51), the cache is not re-checked, so concurrent cold-start requests each perform the full expensive asset computation instead of only one

Mutex guards the cached pointer, not the cached object; GetWebAssets returns the shared *dtos.EntryPointAssets directly, so any caller mutation races against concurrent readers — should return a deep copy on the cached fast path

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds an RWMutex that only protects access to the global pointer `entryPointAssetsCache` (RLock/Lock around reading/assigning the pointer), but `GetWebAssets` returns the cached `*dtos.EntryPointAssets` directly on the fast path (`return ret, nil`) with no copying. That means the cache now shares a mutable object across callers; if any caller mutates the returned struct (or its fields like maps/slices), the mutex does not prevent data races on the object itself. The diff doesn’t prove callers mutate it, so this is an incomplete thread-safety/ownership concern rather than a confirmed defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Cache is globally keyed on nothing and the recompute condition only checks cfg.Env != setting.Dev, so different Cfg values or runtime license changes are never reflected until restart, with no invalidation story documented or tested

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a single global `entryPointAssetsCache` guarded by a mutex, and `GetWebAssets` returns the cached value whenever `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && ret != nil`. The cache is not keyed by `cfg` or `license` (despite both being inputs), so if those inputs can vary at runtime the cached assets would not reflect changes. The diff itself doesn’t establish that `Cfg`/license are expected to change dynamically, so this is a scope/architecture concern rather than a verifiable defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: In Dev mode, the function takes and holds the exclusive write lock for the entire filesystem scan on every request even though the Dev read path bypasses the cache, serializing all Dev requests unnecessarily

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a global RWMutex and unconditionally takes the exclusive Lock() after the early-return check. In Dev mode (`cfg.Env == setting.Dev`), the early return is skipped, so the function will always acquire and hold the write lock (via `defer entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Unlock()`) for the remainder of the function, which likely includes the filesystem scan/build of `result`. This can unnecessarily serialize concurrent Dev requests (a performance/concurrency concern), but it’s not a correctness defect shown in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Missing cache re-check after acquiring the write lock in webassets.go: concurrent cold-start requests serialize on entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock() but each still rebuilds assets, causing N sequential filesystem scans instead of one (partial stampede)

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds an RWMutex and does an initial RLock check (`ret := entryPointAssetsCache` then `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && ret != nil { return ret }`), but after acquiring the write lock it does not re-check whether another goroutine populated `entryPointAssetsCache` while this goroutine was waiting on `Lock()`. From what’s shown, every concurrent cold-start request that observed `nil` under the read lock will proceed past the write lock and rebuild work sequentially, which is a cache-stampede/performance issue rather than a functional correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Global cache ignores the *setting.Cfg parameter of GetWebAssets: first caller's cfg determines cached result, so later callers with different Cfg silently receive wrong assets

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `GetWebAssets` caching results in a single global `entryPointAssetsCache` guarded by a mutex, and the cache lookup only gates on `cfg.Env != setting.Dev` and `entryPointAssetsCache != nil`. There is no keying or invalidation based on other `cfg` fields, so different `*setting.Cfg` inputs would still reuse the same cached value. However, from this diff alone we cannot verify that the computed assets actually vary with `cfg` beyond `Env`, so the claim of “wrong assets” is plausible but not conclusively demonstrated here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Returned *dtos.EntryPointAssets is a shared pointer handed to every request: any handler mutation corrupts responses process-wide, with lock guarding the pointer but not the contents

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a mutex to guard the global `entryPointAssetsCache` pointer, but `GetWebAssets` still returns the cached `*dtos.EntryPointAssets` directly (`ret := entryPointAssetsCache` then `return ret`). The lock only protects swapping/reading the pointer, not concurrent mutation of the pointed-to struct. Whether any caller/handler actually mutates the returned object isn’t shown in this diff, so a concrete bug can’t be verified here, but the shared-mutable-global design concern is real and grounded in the change (also hinted by the TODO).

adjudication_records.issue_text: GetWebAssets holds the exclusive write lock across the entire asset-scan/rebuild work in Dev mode, serializing concurrent Dev-mode requests on a potentially slow filesystem walk; the lock scope is wider than the race requires (compute-then-swap under lock would suffice)

adjudication.rationale: In GetWebAssets, after the initial RLock/RUnlock cache read, the code unconditionally acquires entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock() with a deferred Unlock() before doing the rest of the function’s work (the asset build/scan happens after this point). Since the early return only applies for non-Dev when ret != nil, Dev-mode calls will hold the exclusive lock for the entire rebuild path, serializing concurrent Dev requests. This is a diff-grounded lock-scope/performance concern rather than a correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: GetWebAssets returns the same shared *dtos.EntryPointAssets pointer to all callers across goroutines, so any handler mutating the struct would cause a data race (pre-existing, not introduced by the diff)

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows GetWebAssets caching a global *dtos.EntryPointAssets (entryPointAssetsCache) and returning that same pointer to callers when cfg.Env != setting.Dev (it returns `ret`, which is just the cached pointer). While the new RWMutex protects reads/writes of the cache variable itself, it does not prevent callers from concurrently mutating the returned struct, so sharing a mutable pointer remains a concurrency/design risk. The diff doesn’t prove any caller actually mutates it, so the “would cause a data race” part is speculative.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Read-then-lock pattern is a benign double-checked read of a pointer that can result in redundant work, though not a security failure

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds an RWMutex and performs an initial RLock read (`ret := entryPointAssetsCache`) and early return if non-dev and non-nil, then unconditionally takes the write lock (`entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()`) without re-checking the cache under the write lock. Between the first read and acquiring the write lock, another goroutine could populate `entryPointAssetsCache`, causing redundant recomputation/work. This is a real, diff-grounded concurrency/performance concern but not clearly a functional/security defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Behavioral change to GetWebAssets (replacing racy unsynchronized global read with lock-based double-checked caching) has no accompanying test changes in the diff

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes GetWebAssets caching behavior by introducing a global RWMutex and a double-checked cache read/lock sequence (RLock->read->Unlock, then Lock with deferred Unlock). This is nontrivial behavioral/concurrency logic, and the provided diff shows no accompanying changes to any test files to validate the new caching/locking behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: New double-checked-lock pattern in webassets.go takes the global write Lock unconditionally on cache miss, including every call in Dev mode, risking serializing all Dev-mode requests behind a global mutex (lock convoy on every / asset fetch); it's unclear whether the write-locked body re-checks the cache, so double-computation may occur

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a global RWMutex and performs an initial RLock read, but then takes the write Lock unconditionally after the early-return check. In particular, when `cfg.Env == setting.Dev`, the condition `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && ret != nil` is false even if the cache is populated, so every call will acquire the global write lock and serialize concurrent callers. Also, after dropping the RLock there is no re-check of `entryPointAssetsCache` shown before proceeding under the write lock, so another goroutine could have populated the cache in between, leading to redundant recomputation (performance/efficiency concern rather than a clearly verifiable correctness bug from the shown diff).

adjudication_records.issue_text: No test exists anywhere in the diff covering concurrent Dev-mode calls for the new caching pattern

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces new concurrency-related caching logic via a package-level RWMutex protecting the global `entryPointAssetsCache` and changes the cache read path in `GetWebAssets` (RLock/RUnlock then Lock/defer Unlock). No test code is added in this diff to exercise concurrent calls (including Dev-mode, where caching is bypassed), so the finding about missing coverage for concurrent Dev-mode calls is diff-grounded as a test gap for newly added nontrivial concurrency behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Double-checked locking in GetWebAssets does not re-read entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring the write lock, so concurrent first-callers in non-Dev mode can each rebuild the cache unnecessarily

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, GetWebAssets does an initial RLock read of entryPointAssetsCache into `ret`, then if nil it acquires the write lock but never re-checks `entryPointAssetsCache` after obtaining the lock. This means multiple concurrent callers can all observe `nil` under the read lock, and then (serialized) each proceed past the write lock to rebuild even if an earlier goroutine populated the cache while holding the lock. This is an inefficiency/edge-case in the new locking pattern rather than a functional correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Missing double-check of entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock(), causing concurrent cold-start requests to serially perform redundant full asset scans

adjudication.rationale: In GetWebAssets, the cache is checked under RLock and then the function always takes entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock() when the first check misses. In the shown diff there is no second cache check after acquiring the write lock, so concurrent callers that both observe a nil cache can end up each doing the expensive asset computation sequentially. This is a performance/concurrency efficiency issue (redundant work), not a functional correctness defect, and the rest of the function (not shown) could still include a re-check—so it’s not fully verifiable from the diff snippet alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: Cannot verify whether the freshly computed result is stored back into the cache inside the lock due to truncated diff — a store outside the critical section would be a race

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a Lock() followed immediately by `defer entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Unlock()`, meaning the rest of `GetWebAssets` (including any later cache write in the truncated portion) would execute under the lock unless an explicit unlock occurs later (not shown). The finding’s concern about a write occurring outside the critical section is not supported by what is visible in the diff; it’s speculative based on missing context.
